title: Children and Marital Satisfaction
text:
Many couples expect children to bring them closer. Researchers had been studying the effect of children on marriage for decades, with mixed results. In 2003, Jean Twenge, W. Keith Campbell and Craig Foster combined the findings of nearly a hundred published studies, covering tens of thousands of people, in a meta-analysis.

On average, parents reported lower marital satisfaction than people without children. The difference was modest, but it was consistent, and it followed clear patterns. It was largest among mothers of infants, smaller among fathers, and it grew with the number of children. It was also larger among more affluent couples and in more recent generations, suggesting that the change was felt most by people who had grown used to freedom and an equal sharing of time before children arrived.

The researchers looked at possible reasons. Their analysis suggested that two factors mattered most: conflicts over roles, such as who does what at home now that there is so much more to do, and the loss of freedom, as parents found their time, sleep and spontaneity sharply reduced.

The study did not say that children make people unhappy. It described a specific strain on the couple relationship during the years of intensive care, one that partners can anticipate and work on together.
lesson: Expect children to strain a marriage, especially in the early years, and talk openly about roles and lost freedom. Naming the strain makes it easier to share.
people: Jean Twenge, W. Keith Campbell, Craig Foster
location: San Diego State University, San Diego, USA
source: Twenge, J. M., Campbell, W. K., and Foster, C. A. (2003). Parenthood and marital satisfaction: A meta-analytic review. Journal of Marriage and Family, 65(3), 574-583.
